unit.title: Goals and limits: a model, linear programming in 2D

lesson.title: Choices, limits and a goal
lesson.subtitle: Write a decision with letters and inequalities

video.title: Choices, limits and a goal
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — your science teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the classroom with a lunch plate and a small purse; pupils lean in.
scenes.animation: Food icons pop onto the plate; the purse shrinks.
scenes.narration: Our school kitchen has a problem, and I’ve asked our class to help. Every lunch must give you enough energy, protein and iron, but the money is tight. Can maths find the cheapest plate?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: choices, limits and a goal, written as a model.

scenes.visual: A cup of rice with the letter r beside it, a handful of groundnuts with the letter n.
scenes.animation: Each letter drops onto its food as it is said.
scenes.narration: Start with the choices. How many cups of rice? Call it r. How many handfuls of groundnuts? Call it n. Each letter is a variable: a number you decide, with a unit.

scenes.visual: The inequality builds on a card term by term, then the ≥ 700 lands.
scenes.animation: Terms type in as they are said.
scenes.narration: Now the limits. A cup of rice gives two hundred and sixty kilocalories, a handful of groundnuts one hundred and seventy. Together they must give at least seven hundred. In maths: two hundred and sixty r plus one hundred and seventy n is at least seven hundred.

scenes.visual: Two signs: ≥ with ‘at least’ and ≤ with ‘at most’; examples appear under each.
scenes.animation: Each sign stamps in; examples slide under.
scenes.narration: At least means greater than or equal to. At most means less than or equal to. So iron at least five milligrams, and groundnuts at most two handfuls.

scenes.visual: Price tags on the foods; the cost expression builds; an arrow points down.
scenes.animation: Prices drop onto the expression; the arrow pulses.
scenes.narration: Then the goal: the cost. Rice is fifteen coins a cup, groundnuts eight a handful. Fifteen r plus eight n, as small as possible.

scenes.visual: Three cards snap into one box labelled model.
scenes.narration: Variables, limits and a goal together make a model. Mathematicians call the limits constraints, and the goal the objective.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds a plate with two cups of rice. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Two cups of rice and no groundnuts. Does that meet the energy limit of seven hundred?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; the energy bar stops short of 700; a feasible stamp on another plate.
scenes.animation: Bar fills and stops; stamp lands.
scenes.narration: No: two times two hundred and sixty is five hundred and twenty, less than seven hundred. To check any plan, put its numbers into every limit. A plan that keeps them all is called feasible.

scenes.visual: The usual plate; energy and protein bars full, iron bar short in red; price tag 60.
scenes.animation: Bars fill; the iron bar flashes.
scenes.narration: The usual plate, two cups of rice, an egg and a cup of milk, has plenty of energy and protein. But it has only one point eight milligrams of iron. It isn’t feasible, and it costs sixty coins.

scenes.visual: The 41-coin plate; a classmate shakes her head at the groundnuts; a new rule card slides into the model.
scenes.animation: A warning tag swings in; the rule card lands.
scenes.narration: The cheapest feasible plate costs forty-one coins: rice, groundnuts and a little greens. But what about a classmate who’s allergic to groundnuts? A model only knows the rules you give it, so add the ones that keep everyone safe.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: food buttons, three need bars and a cost.
scenes.animation: A finger taps foods; bars fill.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: School lunch for less
scenes.narration: In the app, build your own plate and watch each need fill up. Then press Find the cheapest. Which needs are met exactly?

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds a card: n __ 2. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The rule says each pupil gets at most two handfuls of groundnuts. Which sign do you write?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets the check; four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Less than or equal to: n is at most two. Remember: a variable is a choice with a unit, a limit is an inequality, and the goal is what you make small or big. To check a plan, put its numbers in.

scenes.visual: A pupil’s notebook: snack names with letters, two inequalities and a goal; two plans ticked and crossed.
scenes.animation: Lines write themselves; a tick and a cross pop.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: write a model for a choice of your own, like snacks for a school trip with your pocket money. Name the variables, write the limits with signs, and the goal. Then check two plans by putting in the numbers.

checkpoints.prompt: Two cups of rice and no groundnuts: does it meet the energy limit of 700?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 2 × 260 = 520, less than 700, so the plate doesn’t fit.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — 2 × 260 = 520, and the limit says at least 700. The price doesn’t change the energy.

checkpoints.prompt: Each pupil gets at most 2 handfuls of groundnuts. Which do you write?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — at most means less than or equal to: n ≤ 2.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — at most means the number can be 2 or less: n ≤ 2.
